name: All Saints' Day
description: A memorial of all believers who have gone before. The hope of resurrection.
biblicalBasis: The great white multitude: "After this I saw a vast crowd that no one could count, from every nation and tribe and people and language. They stood before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes" (Rev 7:9-17). The Beatitudes: "Blessed are the poor in spirit... blessed are those who mourn... blessed are those persecuted for righteousness' sake" (Matt 5:1-12). Hebrews 12:1-2: "Since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses." Jesus' promise: "Whoever believes in me will live, even though they die" (John 11:25-26).
significance: All Saints' Day celebrates not only famous saints but all believers—the unknown grandmother who prayed, the nameless martyr, anyone who lived by faith. Death is not the end; believers are "surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses." The day makes room for both grief and hope: the loss is real, but the hope of resurrection is stronger.
liturgicalContext: White color. Celebrated on the first Sunday in November in the Lutheran tradition. In Norwegian tradition, it is also a memorial day for one's own deceased—candles are lit at graves. Combines festive saintly remembrance with personal grief and hope.
history: The celebration of all saints dates back to the 300s–400s, originally linked to martyr memorials. Pope Gregory III (731) consecrated a chapel to all saints on November 1. The Lutheran tradition kept the day but removed saint worship—the focus shifted to faith as an example and the hope of resurrection.
otConnections: Hebrews 11—witnesses of faith from Abel to the prophets: "All these were commended for their faith." Ezekiel 37 on the dry bones coming to life—the hope of resurrection in the Old Testament. Isaiah 25:6-9: "He will swallow up death forever. The Lord God will wipe away every tear from every face." Daniel 12:2-3 on the resurrection to eternal life.

references.reason: The day is defined by the Beatitudes (Matt 5:1-12) as a central text. The passage describes those who are blessed (believers who have gone before) and offers hope of resurrection and comfort, which lies at the heart of celebrating all believers.
